# Starting from refs and the index only (--no-reflogs), four objects are unreachable:

lines.s: # Overwrite that loose object with a valid zlib stream: same header, same length, other content.
# Ordinary commands read the object by its name and do not recompute the hash:
# git fsck hashes what it finds and compares the result with the file name:
error: bf8a76ba21df71f4f19002c42f44ea784df0f99d: hash-path mismatch, found at:
# A fetch-style transfer rebuilds every ID on the receiving side, so the bad object cannot travel:
fatal: did not receive expected object e2238784c412f0a5151764c07c7a44e7b3a9c073
# A plain file copy has no such check:
# The working tree still holds the true content, and content alone determines the ID.
# Git will not rewrite an object it believes it has, so remove the bad file first.

git add config.toml && git commit --quiet -m 'Add configuration'
# Reflog entries in the past count as starting points. Nothing is dangling:
# Reflog entries dated after "now" are skipped, so the dropped commit looks dangling:

# The commit is in the reflog either way, and the reflog is what you recover from:

slides.text:
Observed behavior : git fsck reports "dangling commit" for a commit that git reflog still lists
Git state         : the only reference to the commit is a reflog entry dated later than the current time
Mechanism         : git fsck notes the time at which it starts and ignores reflog entries newer than that
Root cause        : the entry was written with a committer date in the future: a wrong system clock,
                    or a script that sets GIT_COMMITTER_DATE
Why Git does this : fsck must not be confused by commits that are created while it runs; skipping
                    newer reflog entries is the "coarse solution" its commit message describes
Correct fix       : none is needed; git gc does not apply the rule, and the commit is not deleted
Prevention        : read "dangling" as information; compare with git reflog before pruning anything

beats.text: Why this matters: garbage collection, Git's clean-up, deletes objects, and recovery finds them. Both are defined by one word, reachable. If you can say precisely what is reachable, you know what is safe and for how long.

beats.text: In one sentence: an object is reachable if you can arrive at it from a starting point by following the IDs stored inside objects. git fsck verifies that everything reachable is present and well-formed, and lists what nothing reaches.
beats.tele: In one sentence: an object is reachable if you can arrive at it from a starting point by following the IDs stored inside objects. `git fsck` verifies that everything reachable is present and well-formed, and lists what nothing reaches.

beats.text: Now precisely, in the glossary's words: one object is reachable from another "if we can reach the one from the other by a chain that follows tags to whatever they tag, commits to their parents or trees, and trees to the trees or blobs that they contain".

beats.text: Two more terms. An unreachable object is one that no starting point reaches. A dangling object is an unreachable object that no other unreachable object refers to: the tip of a lost line.
beats.tele: Two more terms. An unreachable object is one that no starting point reaches. A dangling object is an unreachable object that no other unreachable object refers to: the tip of a lost line.

beats.text: The starting points. The manual of git fsck lists them as "the index file, all SHA-1 references in the refs namespace, and all reflogs", and HEAD is added to that. Four roots, then: the index, which is the staging area, all refs, all reflogs, and HEAD, the name for where you are.
beats.tele: The starting points. The manual of `git fsck` lists them as "the index file, all SHA-1 references in the `refs` namespace, and all reflogs", and HEAD is added to that. Four roots, then: the index, which is the staging area, all refs, all reflogs, and HEAD, the name for where you are.

beats.text: Garbage collection keeps the same set alive, and deletes an unreachable object only after a grace period: two weeks by default, the setting gc.pruneExpire.
beats.tele: Garbage collection keeps the same set alive, and deletes an unreachable object only after a grace period: two weeks by default, the setting `gc.pruneExpire`.

says: Garbage collection keeps alive what these four reach

beats.text: Inside .git: git fsck changes nothing. git gc removes unreachable objects from objects/ once they're past the grace period, and git reflog expire removes lines from logs/.
beats.tele: Inside `.git`: `git fsck` changes nothing. `git gc` removes unreachable objects from `objects/` once they're past the grace period, and `git reflog expire` removes lines from `logs/`.

beats.text: The reflog is the root people forget. Reflog entries expire: 90 days by default, and 30 days when the commit is no longer reachable from the tip of the ref. The lab configuration switches both off. And a deleted branch loses its own reflog at once. So after you delete a branch, the entry that still protects its commits is in the reflog of HEAD.
beats.tele: The reflog is the root people forget. Reflog entries expire: 90 days by default, and 30 days when the commit is no longer reachable from the tip of the ref. The lab configuration switches both off. And a deleted branch loses its own reflog at once. So after you delete a branch, the entry that still protects its commits is in the reflog of HEAD.

beats.text: Now the second topic. An object ID is a checksum, and Git doesn't recompute it on every read. A file under objects/ that is a well-formed object with the wrong content is served as it is.
beats.tele: Now the second topic. An object ID is a checksum, and Git doesn't recompute it on every read. A file under `objects/` that is a well-formed object with the wrong content is served as it is.

beats.text: Two operations do recompute IDs from content. git fsck hashes what it finds and compares the result with the name. And a transfer through Git's transport sends object content without IDs. The receiving side computes every ID itself, so an object can't arrive under a name that its content doesn't have. A clone from a local path skips the transport and copies or hard-links the files. The option --no-local forces the transport.
beats.tele: Two operations do recompute IDs from content. `git fsck` hashes what it finds and compares the result with the name. And a transfer through Git's transport sends object content without IDs. The receiving side computes every ID itself, so an object can't arrive under a name that its content doesn't have. A clone from a local path skips the transport and copies or hard-links the files. The option `--no-local` forces the transport.

beats.text: When should you not act? When git fsck prints dangling. That line is information. The lines that are an incident begin with missing or error:.
beats.tele: When should you not act? When `git fsck` prints `dangling`. That line is information. The lines that are an incident begin with `missing` or `error:`.

beats.text: The textbook's analogy is a library with a catalogue. A book is findable if a card names it or a findable book cites it. A book that nothing names is still on its shelf, complete, until the next clear-out.
beats.tele: The textbook's analogy is a library with a catalogue. A book is findable if a card names it or a findable book cites it. A book that nothing names is still on its shelf, complete, until the next clear-out.

beats.text: The analogy breaks at direction. In Git, citations only run from newer to older: a commit names its parents, never its children.
beats.tele: The analogy breaks at direction. In Git, citations only run from newer to older: a commit names its parents, never its children.

beats.text: So losing the card for the newest commit of a line makes the whole line unfindable at once. On screen, the branch from today's demo is deleted, and no branch names its commit any more.
beats.tele: So losing the card for the newest commit of a line makes the whole line unfindable at once. On screen, the branch from today's demo is deleted, and no branch names its commit any more.

beats.text: Try it now, on paper, thirty seconds. Draw three commits in a line, with a branch name on the newest. Erase the name. Which one commit must you find to get all three back? I'll wait.

beats.text: The newest. Carry two consequences from the model. One: "unfindable" is not "gone". The objects stay on the shelf until a clear-out that is weeks away by default. Two: find the newest commit of a lost line, the dangling one, and you have found everything behind it.

beats.text: A healthy repository: no output, exit status 0. Silence is the good answer.

beats.text: Stage a file, then change your mind.

beats.text: A quick quiz. The file was staged and unstaged, and git status shows it as untracked. What does git fsck print now: nothing, an error, or a line about a blob? Your answer?
beats.tele: A quick quiz. The file was staged and unstaged, and `git status` shows it as untracked. What does `git fsck` print now: nothing, an error, or a line about a blob? Your answer?

beats.text: A dangling blob. Unstaging removed an index entry, not the blob that git add had written. Anyone with access to this directory can still read the token. The same fact saves you on the day you lose a staged file.

beats.text: Now a commit on a branch, and then the branch is deleted. Deleting a branch with -D was introduced with its risk label in the branches videos. Here it runs in a sandbox, and the point is what remains afterwards.

beats.text: With the reflogs excluded as starting points: how many objects are unreachable, and how many of them are dangling? Say both numbers out loud. I'll wait.
beats.tele: With the reflogs excluded as starting points: how many objects are unreachable, and how many of them are dangling? Say both numbers out loud. I'll wait.

beats.text: Four are unreachable: the commit, its tree, its new blob, and the blob from the previous step. Two are dangling. The tree 73c1ade and the blob 35376fb aren't dangling, because the unreachable commit refers to them. If you said four and four, that's the usual first answer.

beats.text: The reflog of HEAD still records commit 728ac29. With reflog entries as starting points again, plain git fsck reports only the blob. The commit was never at risk today.
beats.tele: The reflog of HEAD still records commit `728ac29`. With reflog entries as starting points again, plain `git fsck` reports only the blob. The commit was never at risk today.

beats.text: The script then overwrites that loose object file with a valid zlib stream: the same header, the same length, other content. This substitution is crafted. Random damage, such as a flipped bit, normally breaks the zlib stream and fails loudly on the first read.
beats.tele: The script then overwrites that loose object file with a valid zlib stream: the same header, the same length, other content. This substitution is crafted. Random damage, such as a flipped bit, normally breaks the zlib stream and fails loudly on the first read.

beats.text: The content under that ID is now wrong. Will git cat-file complain? Will git status? Yes or no for each. Say it out loud.
beats.tele: The content under that ID is now wrong. Will `git cat-file` complain? Will `git status`? Yes or no for each. Say it out loud.

beats.text: Neither does. Ordinary commands read the object by its name and don't recompute the hash.
beats.tele: Neither does. Ordinary commands read the object by its name and don't recompute the hash.

beats.text: git fsck reports hash-path mismatch and missing blob, with exit status 3. The clone through the transport fails: "did not receive expected object". The clone by file copy succeeds and carries the bad object with it. That is the fourth objective: a corrupt object passes local commands and fails a clone, because only the transfer recomputes every ID.

The clone by file copy succeeds and carries the bad object with it. beats.text: The repair.
beats.tele: The repair.

beats.text: The working tree still holds the true content, and content alone determines the ID. Git won't rewrite an object it believes it has, so the bad file is removed first. Deleting a file under objects/ by hand is damage in every other situation. Here it's the documented repair, for one file that git fsck named. git hash-object -w is 🟢: it adds one object.

Deleting a file under `objects/` by hand is damage in every other situation. Here it's the documented repair, for one file that `git fsck` named. `git hash-object -w` is 🟢: it adds one object.

beats.text: True content in, true ID out: e2238784, as before.
beats.tele: True content in, true ID out: `e2238784`, as before.

beats.text: A small script makes two commits and a reset that drops the second one, all recorded at a given date. It runs twice: once dated 2001, once dated 2099.
beats.tele: A small script makes two commits and a reset that drops the second one, all recorded at a given date. It runs twice: once dated 2001, once dated 2099.

beats.text: The two repositories have the same shape. Will git fsck say the same thing about both, or not? Your answer?
beats.tele: The two repositories have the same shape. Will `git fsck` say the same thing about both, or not? Your answer?

beats.text: It does not. In the repository dated 2099, the dropped commit is reported as dangling, although the reflog lists it.
beats.tele: It does not. In the repository dated 2099, the dropped commit is reported as dangling, although the reflog lists it.

beats.text: The version note: older Git treated every reflog entry as a starting point.
beats.tele: The version note: older Git treated every reflog entry as a starting point.

beats.text: Since Git 2.53.0, entries dated after the moment fsck starts are skipped, and fsck reads the system clock for this. The textbook verified it locally: Git 2.55.0 applies the rule, Apple's Git 2.50.1 does not. So the two Gits on your Mac can disagree about one repository.

beats.text: Last step, the 🔴 command: git gc --prune=now. The five answers. What it changes: it packs the repository and deletes unreachable objects at once, with no grace period. What it can destroy: every unreachable object, which is what recovery depends on. How to preview: git fsck --unreachable, and git prune -n.
beats.tele: Last step, the 🔴 command: `git gc --prune=now`. The five answers. What it changes: it packs the repository and deletes unreachable objects at once, with no grace period. What it can destroy: every unreachable object, which is what recovery depends on. How to preview: `git fsck --unreachable`, and `git prune -n`.

beats.text: How to recover: from another clone or a backup only. When it's appropriate: after a deliberate history rewrite, in a repository you've copied first, never as routine maintenance. Here it runs on a throwaway sandbox to prove one point. Twig looks worried, and with a red label on screen, fairly so.

beats.text: Even with no grace period, the commit stays: garbage collection does not apply the clock rule. And fsck still calls it dangling. "Dangling" is a statement about fsck's starting points, not a verdict.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Running a prune because git fsck printed dangling. Root cause: dangling means no fsck starting point reaches the object; the prune is what destroys recoverable work.
beats.tele: Running a prune because `git fsck` printed `dangling`. Root cause: dangling means no fsck starting point reaches the object; the prune is what destroys recoverable work.

beats.text: Counting on the branch's reflog after deleting the branch. Root cause: a deleted branch loses its own reflog at once; the reflog of HEAD is what still holds the commit.
beats.tele: Counting on the branch's reflog after deleting the branch. Root cause: a deleted branch loses its own reflog at once; the reflog of HEAD is what still holds the commit.

beats.text: Assuming that unstaging a file removes its content. Root cause: git add wrote a blob, and removing the index entry does not remove the object.
beats.tele: Assuming that unstaging a file removes its content. Root cause: `git add` wrote a blob, and removing the index entry does not remove the object.

beats.text: Trusting a local-path clone as an integrity check. Root cause: it copies or hard-links object files and verifies nothing; --no-local forces the transport.
beats.tele: Trusting a local-path clone as an integrity check. Root cause: it copies or hard-links object files and verifies nothing; `--no-local` forces the transport.

beats.text: Two Git versions disagreeing about a repository. Root cause: the future-dated reflog rule exists only in Git 2.53.0 and later.
beats.tele: Two Git versions disagreeing about a repository. Root cause: the future-dated reflog rule exists only in Git 2.53.0 and later.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. An ML platform team keeps a mirror of its training-code repository on the build server and a backup on another host. They run git fsck on a schedule against both, and their runbook has two lines: treat missing and error: lines as an incident, and dangling lines as routine.
beats.tele: Now, out of the lab. An ML platform team keeps a mirror of its training-code repository on the build server and a backup on another host. They run `git fsck` on a schedule against both, and their runbook has two lines: treat `missing` and `error:` lines as an incident, and `dangling` lines as routine.

beats.text: They take the backup through Git's transport, git clone --mirror from a URL or --no-local from a path, when they want every hash recomputed on the way, and as a file copy when they also need reflogs and hooks.
beats.tele: They take the backup through Git's transport, `git clone --mirror` from a URL or `--no-local` from a path, when they want every hash recomputed on the way, and as a file copy when they also need reflogs and hooks.

beats.text: And the same reachability rule is the precise form of an uncomfortable fact about leaked secrets: removing a commit from every branch leaves it in the object database of every clone that has it.
beats.tele: And the same reachability rule is the precise form of an uncomfortable fact about leaked secrets: removing a commit from every branch leaves it in the object database of every clone that has it.
